entry: Result in [[Calculus|calculus]] relating a function's average rate of change over an interval to its instantaneous rate of change. If a real-valued function is [[Continuous function|continuous]] on a closed interval [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), its [[Derivative|derivative]] equals the average rate of change at some point in (a,b). Geometrically, a tangent to the graph is parallel to the secant through the endpoints. [[Augustin-Louis Cauchy]] stated and proved it in modern form in 1823; it is used to prove other properties of differentiable functions.

One of a series of regular sinuous curves in the channel of a stream. It forms as the water erodes [[Sediment|sediment]] from the outer, concave bank and deposits it on the inner, convex bank, so that the channel migrates back and forth across the [[Floodplain|floodplain]]. Meanders migrate downstream over time, which can create [[Civil engineering|civil engineering]] challenges for maintaining roads and bridges. The degree of meandering is measured by sinuosity, the ratio of channel length to straight-line down-valley distance; a single-channel [[River|river]] with a sinuosity of 1.5 or more is defined as meandering. The term derives from the winding Menderes River in Asia Minor, which the Greeks called Maiandros.

Philosophical question of whether an individual's life, human life or existence in general has inherent significance. There is no consensus on the answer, or on whether such significance exists in any objective sense. Proposed answers come from many cultures and ideologies, drawing on philosophy, religion and science. [[Arthur Schopenhauer]] was the first to ask the question explicitly, in an essay titled "Character." Supernaturalism locates meaning in divine or supernatural sources, naturalism in the natural world, and [[Nihilism|nihilism]] denies any inherent meaning. [[Existentialism|Existentialist]] thinkers such as [[Albert Camus]] and [[Friedrich Nietzsche]] explored the question, and psychological research links a sense of purpose to better mental health and resilience.

Sense or significance of an entity, expressing what it conveys or stands for. Meaning is a relational concept linking a sign to what it signifies; the word *dog*, for example, connects to a four-legged animal. Philosophers study linguistic meaning, including the relation between sense and reference and the difference between what an expression conventionally means and what a speaker intends. Theories of meaning include referential theories, associated with [[Gottlob Frege]] and [[Bertrand Russell]], and mental theories that explain meaning through ideas or communicative intentions; [[John Locke]] treated words as signs of ideas. Meaning is also attributed to pictures, [[Map|maps]] and actions. The study of meaning is central to [[Philosophy of language|philosophy of language]] and informs [[Semiotics|semiotics]] and [[Philosophy of mind|philosophy of mind]]. The [[Meaning of life|meaning of life]] is a related non-linguistic sense concerned with the significance of human existence as a whole.

Highly contagious viral [[Infection|infection]] caused by the measles virus, which is closely related to rinderpest and canine distemper. Initial symptoms of fever, cough, runny nose and [[Conjunctivitis|inflamed eyes]] appear 10–12 days after exposure, followed by a rash that starts on the face and spreads over the body. Complications include [[Diarrhea|diarrhea]], middle ear infection and [[Pneumonia|pneumonia]], and less commonly [[Encephalitis|brain inflammation]]. Measles spreads through the air, and immunity is lifelong after [[Vaccination|vaccination]] or recovery. No specific antiviral treatment exists; care focuses on preventing secondary infections, hydration and pain relief. Herd immunity requires more than 95% of a community to be vaccinated. Vaccination cut measles deaths by 80% from 2000 to 2017, but progress has stalled since the [[COVID-19 pandemic]]. Measles currently causes an estimated 95 thousand deaths a year, mainly in countries with low per capita income and poor health systems.

American singer and actor. Born Marvin Lee Aday in [[Dallas]], [[Texas]]. His *Bat Out of Hell* album trilogy has sold more than 100 million records worldwide. He won a Grammy Award for Best Solo Rock Vocal Performance for "I'd Do Anything for Love." He had greater success in Europe, especially the United Kingdom and Ireland, than in the United States. He appeared in over 50 films and television shows, including Eddie in *The Rocky Horror Picture Show* (1975) and Robert "Bob" Paulsen in *Fight Club* (1999).

Skilled tradesperson who uses [[Tool|tools]] to build, maintain, repair and improve [[Machine|machinery]], especially [[Vehicle|vehicles]]. The term once referred to any [[Handicraft|handicraft]] trade but has meant machinery work since the early 20th century. Mechanics work in automotive, aeronautical, maritime, mining, military and many other fields, inspecting equipment, diagnosing faults and replacing components. Training combines practical experience with apprenticeship, vocational education or certification. The profession grew rapidly during the [[Industrial Revolution]].

Branch of [[Physics|physics]] concerned with the relationships between force, matter and motion among physical objects. Forces may cause displacements, which are changes in an object's position relative to its environment. Theoretical work on the subject began in ancient Greece, where philosophers were among the first to propose that abstract principles govern nature, and the main theory of mechanics in antiquity was Aristotelian mechanics. A parallel tradition used mathematics more extensively to analyze bodies statically or dynamically. Early modern scientists, including [[Galileo Galilei]], Johannes Kepler, Christiaan Huygens and [[Isaac Newton]], laid the foundation for [[Classical mechanics|classical mechanics]]. In the 20th century, new discoveries challenged these concepts and led to [[Relativistic mechanics|relativistic mechanics]] and [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]].

Process of changing from work done largely or exclusively by hand or with animals to work done with [[Machine|machinery]]. An early engineering text defined a machine as something interposed between a moving power and the work to be done, adapting one to the other. In modern usage, as in engineering or economics, mechanization implies machinery more complex than hand tools, and would not include simple devices such as an ungeared horse or donkey mill. Devices that change speed or convert reciprocating motion to rotary motion, using means such as [[Gear|gears]], [[Pulley|pulleys]], belts, cams and cranks, are usually considered machines. After electrification, when most small machinery was no longer hand powered, mechanization became synonymous with motorized machines. The extension of mechanization into production is termed [[Automation|automation]], controlled by a closed-loop system in which sensors provide feedback.

City (pop., 2020: 2,435,252), capital of the [[Indonesia|Indonesian]] province of North Sumatra. Its nearby [[Strait of Malacca]], Port of Belawan and Kualanamu International Airport make it a regional hub. About 60% of North Sumatra's economy is backed by trade, agriculture and processing industries. The city was founded at the confluence of the Deli and Babura rivers by a Karonese man, Guru Patimpus, and became part of the Deli Sultanate, established in 1632. Dutch colonists chose Medan and Deli as plantation hubs for the Deli Company in the late 19th century. The Dutch [[Tobacco|tobacco]] trade made it an economic hub, earning it the nickname *Het Land Dollar* ("the land of the money"). It is the most populous city in Indonesia outside [[Java]].

Sorceress in [[Greek mythology]], daughter of King Aeëtes of Colchis. She first appears in [[Hesiod|Hesiod's]] *Theogony* around 700 BC and is best known from [[Euripides|Euripides's]] 5th-century BC tragedy *Medea*. In the myth of the Argonauts she helps Jason win the Golden Fleece, but in Euripides's version she murders her sons and Jason's new bride after Jason plans to abandon her. According to [[Herodotus]], she later settled on the Iranian plateau, where the Aryans became known as the [[Medes]].

City (pop., 2018: 2,427,129), capital of the department of Antioquia and the second-largest city in [[Colombia]] after [[Bogotá]]. It lies in the Aburrá Valley of the [[Andes]]. Founded as a town in 1675, it was a commercial center in the 19th century, first exporting gold and then coffee. Its metro area, with more than 4 million people, produces 67% of Antioquia's GDP. Construction of the Medellín Metro commuter rail, liberalized development policies, and better security and education revived industrial dynamism from the late 20th century. The Urban Land Institute named it the most innovative city in the world in 2013, and it won the Lee Kuan Yew World City Prize in 2016.

Confederation of Colombian drug-trafficking organizations based mainly in [[Medellín]]. It played a central role in expanding the international [[Cocaine|cocaine]] trade in the late 1970s and 1980s. Rather than a single hierarchy, it was a network of semi-autonomous traffickers, including [[Pablo Escobar]]. Some members used assassinations, bombings and intimidation against judges, politicians and journalists to oppose extradition to the United States, a strategy described in Colombian scholarship as narcoterrorism. Key figures were killed or arrested as the network was dismantled in the late 1980s and early 1990s.

Iron Age [[Iran|Iranian]] people who spoke the Median language and inhabited Media, between western and northern Iran. Around the 11th century BC they occupied northwestern Iran and parts of [[Mesopotamia]], near Ecbatana (present-day Hamadan). Their consolidation in Iran is believed to have occurred in the 8th century BC. Accounts by [[Herodotus]] portray a powerful people who played a pivotal role in the fall of the Assyrian Empire and competed with [[Lydia]] and [[Babylonia]]. The Medes left no written records, and some specialists doubt there was ever a powerful Median kingdom. After the last Median king fell to [[Cyrus the Great]], Media became an important province prized by successive empires.

American [[Civil rights movement|civil rights]] activist and the first field secretary of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) in Mississippi. He challenged segregation at the University of Mississippi by applying to its law school after the 1954 Brown v. Board of Education ruling. He was murdered at his home in [[Jackson, Mississippi|Jackson]] by Byron De La Beckwith, a member of the White Citizens' Council. De La Beckwith was convicted in 1994 on new evidence, after all-white juries failed to reach verdicts in trials during the 1960s. His widow, Myrlie Evers, later served as national chair of the NAACP.

Middle value of a data set, separating its higher half from its lower half. The median applies to a data sample, a population or a [[Probability distribution|probability distribution]]. Unlike the mean, or [[Average|average]], it is not skewed by a small proportion of extreme values, so it gives a better representation of the center. Median income, for example, may describe the center of the income distribution better than the mean. Increases in the largest incomes alone have no effect on the median. Because of this, the median is of central importance in robust statistics. As a 2-quantile, it partitions a set into two equal parts.

Process of determining which disease or condition explains a person's symptoms and signs, abbreviated Dx. The information is typically collected from a history and [[Physical examination|physical examination]], often supplemented by [[Medical test|medical tests]]. Diagnosis is often difficult because many signs are nonspecific: redness of the skin (erythema), for example, is a sign of many disorders. Clinicians therefore compare possible explanations in a differential diagnosis, correlating information and recognizing patterns. Occasionally a pathognomonic sign or symptom makes the process easy. From a statistical view, diagnosis involves classification tests. Diagnosis is a major component of a doctor's visit, and studies of patient outcomes after diagnosis form the field of survival epidemiology.

Health professional who practices [[Medicine|medicine]], also called a physician (American and Canadian English) or medical practitioner (British English). Medicine aims to promote, maintain or restore health through the study, diagnosis, prognosis and treatment of disease, injury and other physical and mental conditions. Doctors may focus on particular disease categories, types of patients or methods of treatment, known as specialties, or work in general practice, providing continuing and comprehensive care to individuals and families. Practice requires thorough knowledge of [[Anatomy|anatomy]] and [[Physiology|physiology]], as well as the competence to apply it. [[Medical ethics|Medical ethics]] requires doctors to show consideration, compassion and benevolence toward patients, although the role and title vary around the world.

Applied branch of [[Ethics|ethics]] that analyzes clinical medicine and related scientific research. It rests on respect for autonomy, non-maleficence, beneficence and justice, which are not ranked in order of importance, although conflicts may require some principles to outweigh others. Major codes include the Hippocratic Oath, which dates to the fifth century BCE, the Nuremberg Code (1947) and the Declaration of Helsinki (1964). Issues include [[Euthanasia|euthanasia]], patient confidentiality, informed consent and the treatment of patients who lack decision-making capacity. The overturning of [[Roe v. Wade]] by the Supreme Court in 2022 raised the question of whether doctors should be legally punished for providing an [[Abortion|abortion]] to save a patient's life. Because cultures apply ethical values differently, culturally sensitive physicians and ethics committees are increasingly needed.

Technique of imaging the interior of a body for clinical analysis, medical intervention and visual representation of organ function. Medical imaging reveals internal structures hidden by the skin and bones, helps diagnose and treat disease, and builds a database of normal [[Anatomy|anatomy]] and [[Physiology|physiology]] against which abnormalities can be identified. Imaging of removed organs is usually considered part of [[Pathology|pathology]]. As of 2010, 5 billion medical imaging studies had been conducted worldwide. In 2006, medical imaging accounted for about 50% of total [[Ionizing radiation|ionizing radiation]] exposure in the United States. The equipment uses semiconductor technology, including [[Integrated circuit|integrated circuit]] chips and sensors; annual shipments of imaging chips reached 46 million units and $1.1 billion in 2015. Most imaging techniques are noninvasive, meaning no instrument is introduced into the body.

Medical procedure performed to detect, diagnose or monitor diseases, disease processes or susceptibility, or to determine a course of treatment. Tests include [[Physical examination|physical]] and visual examinations, diagnostic imaging, genetic testing, and chemical and cellular analysis. They are typically performed in a medical setting. Tests are classified by purpose as diagnostic, screening or monitoring. A diagnostic test confirms or determines the presence of disease in a person suspected of having it, usually after symptoms are reported. For example, measuring blood sugar after periods of increased urination can test for [[Diabetes|diabetes]]. Screening tests, such as blood pressure measurements or cholesterol panels, detect preclinical conditions in healthy populations. Laboratory tests analyze [[Blood test|blood]], urine or tissue samples, while [[X-ray|X-rays]] visualize internal structures.

Diagnostic and therapeutic use of [[Ultrasound|ultrasound]], mainly for imaging. It creates images of internal structures such as [[Tendon|tendons]], [[Muscle|muscles]], joints, blood vessels and organs, and can measure distances and velocities. The practice of examining pregnant women with ultrasound, called obstetric ultrasonography, was an early development of clinical ultrasonography. Ultrasound consists of sound waves with frequencies greater than 20,000 Hz, the approximate upper threshold of human hearing. A probe sends pulses of ultrasound into tissue, and the echoes that return are displayed as an image called a sonogram. Most examinations use a transducer on the body's surface, but special transducers placed inside the body, such as transvaginal and transesophageal ones, often give better views.

Discipline at the intersection of [[Chemistry|chemistry]] and [[Pharmacy|pharmacy]] concerned with designing and developing drugs. It identifies, synthesizes and develops new chemical entities for therapeutic use, and studies the biological properties of existing drugs and their quantitative structure-activity relationships. Most medicines are [[Organic compound|organic compounds]], including small molecules such as [[Atorvastatin|atorvastatin]] and protein-based biologics such as insulin glargine. Metal-based agents include [[Platinum|platinum]], [[Lithium|lithium]] and gallium compounds, such as cisplatin, lithium carbonate and gallium nitrate. The field combines [[Organic chemistry|organic chemistry]] with biochemistry, computational chemistry, [[Pharmacology|pharmacology]], molecular biology, statistics and physical chemistry. Pharmaceutical chemistry focuses on the quality of medicines and their fitness for purpose.

Sacred and secular music of Western Europe during the [[Middle Ages]], roughly the 6th to 15th centuries. It is the first and longest major era of [[Classical music|Western classical music]], followed by [[Renaissance music]]. Musicologists group these eras as early music, which precedes the common practice period. Medieval music is traditionally divided into Early (500–1150), High (1150–1300) and Late (1300–1400) periods. It includes liturgical music for the church, other sacred music and secular music. Much of it is purely vocal, such as [[Gregorian chant]], while other works used only instruments or combined voices and instruments. The period saw the creation of systems of [[Musical notation|notation]] that let composers document and transmit music, although notation coexisted with oral tradition.

Philosophy of the [[Middle Ages]], extending from the fall of the Western Roman Empire in the 5th century. Medieval philosophy as independent inquiry began in Baghdad in the mid-8th century, and in the court of [[Charlemagne]] at [[Aachen]] in the last quarter of that century. It was shaped by the rediscovery of ancient Greek and Roman thought and by the need to integrate sacred doctrine with secular learning. God was the central concern of Jewish, Christian and Muslim thinkers alike. Major problems included the relation of [[Faith|faith]] to [[Reason|reason]], the existence and simplicity of God, and universals. The 12th to 14th centuries in the Latin West were a "golden age", when the recovery of ancient philosophy culminated, aided by Arabic commentators. Renaissance humanists later dismissed the Scholastic period as a barbaric "middle period".
